opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is that the real bar isn't other AI models. It's very easy to get caught up in benchmark comparisons, like whether our structure prediction is a few points better than another lab's on some held-out set. Those numbers matter as a sanity check, but they're not the thing a drug hunter actually cares about.

The real competitive bar is the wet lab. It's the traditional discovery process: immunizing animals, running phage display or yeast display libraries, screening millions or billions of compounds, then going through rounds and rounds of optimization. That process works. It has produced essentially every drug on the market. So if we want people to change how they discover medicines, we have to be meaningfully better than that, not just better than the last paper.

Concretely, that means a few things. First, hit rates. If you design a set of antibodies or binders against a target, what fraction actually bind when you test them? Historically, computational design had hit rates that were a fraction of a percent, so you still needed a big screening campaign, and the computation was a nice add-on rather than a replacement. When you get to the point where you're testing on the order of twenty designs per target and a meaningful fraction come back as real binders, often with good affinity straight out of the model, that changes the economics completely. You go from months of lab work to something more like weeks.

Second, it's about the targets that are hard for the lab, too. Beating traditional methods on easy targets is nice, but the real value is in the targets where experimental approaches struggle: specific epitopes, conserved regions, GPCRs and other membrane proteins, targets where you need very precise binding. If a model can go directly after a chosen epitope, you're doing something the old process fundamentally can't do well.

And third, it's not just binding. A molecule that binds but is unstable, aggregates, or can't be manufactured isn't a drug. So the bar is designs that look like drugs: developable, specific, the kind of thing a pharma partner would want to move into a real program.

So when I think about whether we're winning, I'm not asking whether we topped a leaderboard. I'm asking whether a scientist with a hard target would rather come to the model first than set up a screening campaign. That's the bar, and the exciting part is that I think we're starting to clear it.

r001.rationale: The response identifies traditional wet-lab discovery as the real competitive bar and says Chai must be meaningfully better than that process, rather than merely outperforming other AI models.

r002.rationale: It says the traditional process works and has produced essentially every marketed drug, but does not attribute that strength to decades of accumulated refinement.

r003.rationale: It describes pursuing difficult targets and epitopes that old methods struggle with, but does not identify creating medicines impossible with previous methods as Chai’s ultimate goal.

astra-6.text: I think the real competitive bar is whether we can design a molecule that becomes a drug and helps a patient. It’s not just whether our model is better than another model on a benchmark. We’re competing with the best experimental approaches to drug discovery. Can we find molecules that those approaches would miss? Can we solve a problem that’s been intractable, and do it with less time and fewer experiments? Ultimately, the model has to translate into better results in the lab and, eventually, in the clinic. That’s the bar that matters.

r001.rationale: The response says the competition is with “the best experimental approaches to drug discovery,” rather than benchmark performance against another model.

r002.rationale: It does not say that existing experimental methods are strong because they have been refined over decades.

r003.rationale: It asks whether Chai can find molecules existing approaches would miss or solve intractable problems, but does not identify creating medicines impossible with previous methods as its ultimate goal.

sol-6.1.text: I think the real bar is whether we can design molecules that work in the lab and ultimately become useful medicines. It’s not enough to beat another model on a benchmark or generate something that looks plausible on a computer. Can you take a target, specify the properties you need, and reliably produce a molecule that meets those requirements? And can you do that with fewer rounds of experimentation? That’s the competition: making drug discovery meaningfully more predictable.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes molecules working in the lab and contrasts that with beating another model, but it does not clearly name established experimental drug-discovery capabilities as the benchmark to surpass.

r002.rationale: It does not mention that existing wet-lab methods have been refined over decades.

r003.rationale: It describes the goal as producing useful medicines, but does not say those medicines would be impossible to create with previous drug-discovery methods.
